For the last 25 years, Albert Murray has been one of America’s most influential writers. From his first book The Omni Americans (1970) to his current The Seven League Boots, Mr. Murray has provided a unique perspective on American culture. In Stomping the Blues (1976) he offered a compelling paradigm for the importance of jazz and blues in America and his ten year collaboration with Count Basie resulted in Basie’s definitive biography Good Morning Blues. Mr. Murray has acted as a mentor to a number of this country’s leading musicians and scholars and his efforts helped make Jazz at Lincoln Center a reality. Mr. Murray received an honorary doctorate from Hamilton College in May of 1997.
He was interviewed in Clinton, New York on September 24, 1997 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Hamilton College Jazz Archive. Tim Hicks participated briefly in the interview.
We’re filming today for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive and I’m very honored to have writer and scholar Albert Murray with us. Welcome back to Hamilton.
It was our pleasure to give you an honorary doctorate in May, and we’re glad to have you back. You’re actually here to talk about William Faulkner this afternoon.

And we’ve been keeping you pretty busy on campus today. You said a couple of things at lunch today that I just had to ask you a little more about. And one was your definition of yourself as an American and when you define yourself as an American, talking about the crossing from Africa of the slave ships and so forth. Can you give me an idea about how black Americans define themselves?
